solution:
Convert the side to SI: \(a = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\), so the area of the square is \(A = a^{2} = (0.10\,\text{m})^{2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\).

For a uniform field the flux through a flat surface is \(\Phi = \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{A} = EA\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{E}\) and the NORMAL to the surface (not the surface itself). Here \(E = 3 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\).

(a) A plane parallel to the \(yz\) plane has its normal along the \(x\)-axis, i.e. along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\), so \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) and the field passes squarely through the square:
\(\Phi = (3 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N C}^{-1})(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2})\cos 0^{\circ} = 30\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\).

(b) Tilting the square so that its normal makes \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\) with the \(x\)-axis reduces the projected area by \(\cos 60^{\circ} = 0.5\):
\(\Phi = (3 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N C}^{-1})(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2})\cos 60^{\circ} = 30 \times 0.5 = 15\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\).

(a) \(\Phi = 30\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)
(b) \(\Phi = 15\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)

The field of Exercise 1.14 is \(\mathbf{E} = 3 \times 10^{3}\,\hat{\mathbf{i}}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), uniform and directed along the \(x\)-axis. The cube has edge \(a = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\), so each face has area \(A = (0.20\,\text{m})^{2} = 4.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\).

Take the six faces one at a time, each with its OUTWARD normal.

The four faces parallel to the \(x\)-axis (the two \(xy\) faces and the two \(xz\) faces) have outward normals along \(\pm\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(\pm\hat{\mathbf{k}}\), which are perpendicular to \(\mathbf{E}\). Each contributes \(EA\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\).

The two faces perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis have outward normals \(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (the face the field enters) and \(+\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (the face it leaves), giving
\(\Phi_{\text{in}} = -EA = -(3 \times 10^{3})(4.0 \times 10^{-2}) = -1.2 \times 10^{2}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\) and
\(\Phi_{\text{out}} = +EA = +1.2 \times 10^{2}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\).

These cancel exactly, so the net flux is zero. Physically, whatever field lines enter the cube on one side leave it on the other: a uniform field has no source or sink, so no line begins or ends inside. The same result follows at once from Gauss's law, \(\Phi = q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_{0}\), since there is no charge inside the cube. Note this is independent of the edge length and of where the cube is placed.

Net flux through the cube \(= 0\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)

(a) Gauss's law relates the net outward flux through a closed surface to the charge it encloses: \(\Phi = q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_{0}\), so \(q_{\text{enc}} = \varepsilon_{0}\Phi\).

With \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}\) and \(\Phi = 8.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\):
\(q_{\text{enc}} = (8.854 \times 10^{-12})(8.0 \times 10^{3}) = 7.08 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\).

The flux is outward (positive), so the enclosed charge is positive, about \(0.071\,\mu\text{C}\).

(b) No, one could not. Gauss's law fixes only the NET charge enclosed, because the flux counts field lines with a sign: a line leaving contributes positively and a line entering negatively. Zero net flux therefore means the positive and negative charges inside are equal in magnitude, not that there is no charge at all. A dipole placed inside the box, or any pair of equal and opposite charges, would give exactly zero net flux while the box plainly contains charge; the field on the surface would not vanish, it would merely be outward over part of the surface and inward over the rest, in equal measure. The only safe conclusion from zero net flux is \(q_{\text{enc}} = 0\).

(a) \(q_{\text{enc}} = 7.08 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C} \approx 0.071\,\mu\text{C}\) (positive)
(b) No. Zero net flux means only that the net enclosed charge is zero; equal positive and negative charges (e.g. a dipole) inside the box would also give zero flux.

The value printed against 1.17 is the correct answer to 1.18, and the value printed against 1.18 is the correct answer to THIS question. That is what identifies it as a single transposition rather than two unrelated slips — each printed number is right, just filed under the other question. The answer below is derived independently.] Follow the hint. The charge sits \(5\,\text{cm}\) directly above the centre of a square of side \(10\,\text{cm}\). Imagine a cube of edge \(10\,\text{cm}\) having this square as one face and extending upward: its centre lies on the perpendicular through the square's centre at a height of half the edge, i.e. \(10/2 = 5\,\text{cm}\). That is exactly where the charge is, so the charge is at the CENTRE of the cube.

By Gauss's law the total flux through the whole closed cube is
\(\Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\).

The six faces are equivalent by symmetry about the centre, so each carries one sixth of it:
\(\Phi_{\text{face}} = \dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_{0}}\).

In SI, \(q = +10\,\mu\text{C} = 10 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{C}\), and \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}\):
\(\Phi_{\text{face}} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-5}}{5.312 \times 10^{-11}} = 1.88 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\).

The side lengths never enter the final expression; only the fact that the charge sits at the cube's centre does.

Flux through the square \(= 1.88 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key's entries for Exercises 1.17 and 1.18 are TRANSPOSED — see the note on 1.17. The value printed against 1.18 is the correct answer to 1.17, and the answer to THIS question is the one printed against 1.17. Each printed number is correct; only the two are swapped.] By Gauss's law the net flux through any closed surface depends only on the charge enclosed:
\(\Phi = \dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\).

In SI, \(q = 2.0\,\mu\text{C} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}\), and taking \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}\):
\(\Phi = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.26 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\).

The edge length \(9.0\,\text{cm}\) is not needed and does not appear: the flux is the same for a cube of any size, and indeed for any closed surface, as long as the same charge is inside. (Enlarging the surface weakens \(E\) as \(1/r^{2}\) but enlarges the area as \(r^{2}\), so the product is unchanged.)

Net flux through the cube \(= 2.26 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)

(a) By Gauss's law, \(\Phi = q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_{0}\), the flux through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge, not on the size or shape of the surface. Doubling the radius from \(10.0\,\text{cm}\) to \(20.0\,\text{cm}\) encloses the same point charge, so the flux is unchanged. (Explicitly: the field falls as \(1/r^{2}\) while the spherical area grows as \(4\pi r^{2}\), and the two factors of \(r^{2}\) cancel.)

Flux through the enlarged surface \(= -1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\), the same as before.

(b) Rearranging Gauss's law, \(q = \varepsilon_{0}\Phi\). With \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}\) and \(\Phi = -1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\):
\(q = (8.854 \times 10^{-12})(-1.0 \times 10^{3}) = -8.85 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C} = -8.85\,\text{nC}\).

The minus sign is physical, not bookkeeping: a negative flux means the field is directed INWARD through the outward-facing normal everywhere on the sphere, i.e. field lines terminate on the charge rather than starting from it. That is the signature of a negative charge, which is what the sign of \(q\) confirms. The radius \(10.0\,\text{cm}\) is not needed for either part.

(a) \(\Phi = -1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}\) (unchanged)
(b) \(q = -8.85 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C} \approx -8.9\,\text{nC}\)
